source_evidence.span: Duo traduntur huius genera, alterum aculeatum, alterum minime, hortense utrumque.
source_evidence.consequence: Two described types both have cultivated status while thorn status differs. Cultivated does not entail thornless.

source_evidence.span: Altera species priori ex omniparte similis est, nisi quod aculeis caret. Ad cibos plus quam altera expetitur.
source_evidence.consequence: The second type lacks thorns and is more sought for food. Shared cultivation, thorn difference and comparative food preference must remain separate predicates.
Tragus identifies this counterpart as Columella's Cinara; this is an attributed naming claim, not a universal uncontested alias.

source_evidence.span: Utrumque genus ... Columella; Hispida ponatur Cinara; spinisque ... horret.
source_evidence.consequence: Lonitzer presents the following Columella verse as embracing both types. The verse itself uses Cinara with prickly imagery; it cautions against making every Cinara occurrence mean thornless. It does not independently establish modern type identity.

source_evidence.span: Graeci hoc faciunt discrimen, quod scolymos est ferus et silvester, Cinara vero domita cultu, ruditate mitior et altilis.
source_evidence.consequence: The distinction is explicitly attributed to Greeks: wild Scolymos versus Cinara tamed by cultivation. It states no thornless equivalence and does not erase the opening use of Scolymos in a cultivated account.

source_evidence.span: Praeterea silvestris est quaedam Cardui species ... foliis aculeatis ... capitulis aculeatis ... flore in quibusdam purpureo, in quibusdam albo, in quibusdam puniceo.
source_evidence.consequence: A wild type is separately introduced, with thorny leaves/heads and multiple stated flower colors. Wild occurrence is not the owner of every earlier naming/use clause.

source_evidence.span: Silvestris ... idem temperamentum; Radices ... hieme eduntur; Radix illita ... emendat; Carduus hortensis cui spina est mollior arte.
source_evidence.consequence: Wild and preceding Scolymon share temperament, so that quality does not separate them here. Root food/topical uses and the Fiera poem do not independently attach to each of the opening two cultivated variants; the softened-thorn poem does not describe an observed temporal conversion of one specimen.

retained_counterexamples: Carduus cultivated-and-thorny directly contradicts CULTIVATED implies NOT_THORNY.
Carduus cultivated thornless counterpart contradicts any whole-class rule requiring all Carduus subjects to carry the same thorn status.
Dipsacus cultivated heads are MORE prickly than spontaneous heads (complete entry lines10–12); a global wild-implies-more-prickly polarity is false in this retained source comparison.
Carduus wild flower colors include white and purple as well as red; the Dipsacus white-cultivated/purple-spontaneous color pairing is not a transferable universal cultivation code.
Scolymos appears at the opening cultivated Carduus account as well as in the Greek-attributed wild distinction; a global Scolymos-implies-wild assignment discards authority/context.
The certified lower71v illustration belongs to the separate wild discussion. It is not certified as the spineless cultivated counterpart; prior native record only, no image opened.

available_meaning_consequences.ceiling: A source-constrained hypothesis; no target form, owner or construction currently binds these values.
